items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 16, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including a joint call by Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK on Israel to allow urgent humanitarian aid into Gaza, the reported deployment of a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and the interception of drones over Saudi Arabia amid escalating tensions with Yemen's Houthis. The foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom urged Israel to "stop the delays now" and permit the immediate entry of 150,000 tents and critical supplies into Gaza ahead of winter. "We ... are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire," the top diplomats said in a joint statement. Noting that recent flooding from the first winter storm has compounded civilian suffering, the ministers warned that border restrictions are blocking desperately needed shelter and relief materials. They stressed that the crisis remains "entirely reversible" before harsher weather sets in, calling on Israel to open border crossings and grant entry to "dual-use items" required for humanitarian operations and early recovery "before it is too late." The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt will join two other US aircraft carriers in the Middle East within the next day, bringing the total American carrier presence in the region to three, the New York Times reported, citing a US military official. The deployment comes as Iran launched a drone attack against Bahrain on Sunday for the second time in three days, ending a roughly two-month lull in hostilities while peace negotiations with Washington remain stalled. The strike followed an incident on Friday in which US forces intercepted two Iranian drones headed toward the Gulf nation. Neither the Pentagon nor the US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has issued an official confirmation regarding the carrier's deployment schedule.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal linked the attack to his country’s support for Ukraine, saying the closures would reduce the risk of further sabotage. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the measures would also help prevent sanctions circumvention. Russia rejected the accusations, describing the decision as “Russophobia”. ... Southeast Asian leaders have extended restrictions on Myanmar’s political representation at regional summits, citing continued violence and failure to implement a peace plan adopted after the 2021 military coup. Washington has not confirmed the proposal, with a US official saying several ideas remain under discussion and any agreement would require both sides’ consent. Zelenskyy said he would put a specific proposal to Ukrainians if it included credible security guarantees, no restrictions on Ukraine’s military and reconstruction funding. He said he could not decide the territorial question alone. Russia controls most of Donbas and has demanded Ukraine surrender the remaining territory as a condition for peace. The comments follow meetings between US envoys and leaders in Kyiv and Moscow, as negotiations continue over ending Russia’s invasion. NATO membership has long been sought by Ukraine but opposed by Moscow, while other alliance members have also expressed reservations about admitting Kyiv. The San Francisco Declaration includes Japan, Australia, Israel, the UK, South Korea, India, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission are expected to sign next week. The agreement forms part of Pax Silica, a US-led initiative covering semiconductors, critical minerals, energy and related infrastructure. US Under-Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg said partners would jointly identify sensitive technologies and share information about supply chains requiring diversification. Working groups will also explore investment hubs and safeguards against technology theft. ... SpaceX has captured a Starship spacecraft returning from orbit using mechanical arms at its Texas launch tower, the first successful recovery of the upper-stage vehicle. The spacecraft returned on Saturday, 22 hours after launch, following 14 orbits of Earth at an altitude of about 265 kilometres. It also deployed 26 Starlink satellites. The mission was not a complete success. The first-stage booster exploded during its attempted return after its engines stopped firing too early. SpaceX said its guidance system diverted the booster away from the launch site and initiated self-destruction. Engineers are investigating the failure, although three boosters had previously been caught successfully. SpaceX said the spacecraft’s heat shield and other systems performed well.

items.title: Fed 'has some work to do on inflation,' Kansas City Fed chief says
items.excerpt: Published Sun, Nov 15 2026 1:58 PM EST Updated Sun, Nov 15 2026 2:04 PM EST ... The Federal Reserve has the tools and responsibility to address price pressures that are "running too hot," and the central bank "has some work to do on inflation," Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said Sunday. Schmid, speaking to a credit union conference in Hawaii, did not specifically call for additional rate hikes, but said inflation is "uncomfortably above the 2% price stability target, and moving in the wrong direction." Common narratives that have recently evolved around the nature of current inflation and the Fed's ability to contain it are off-base, Schmid said. First, Schmid said, the view that high inflation is a reflection of repeated supply shocks neglects that "inflation is always the result of an imbalance between supply and demand. It is in the context of strong demand that a disruption to supply drives up prices. Demand always plays a role in inflation, and the Fed, through its influence on demand, always has the tools and responsibility to address inflation." Schmid, who is not a Federal Open Market Committee voting member this year, said he also disagrees with the narrative that the sources of demand-induced inflation right now — like the artificial intelligence buildout — are resistant to Fed policy. The Fed raised rates by a quarter-percentage point in September to 3.75%-4.00% but opted not to lift them again at last month's meeting. After recent inflation readings came in higher than expected and comments from other Fed officials, including influential Governor Christopher Waller, interest rate futures markets are now fully priced for a quarter-point increase at December's meeting, with a small probability of a half-point hike. "I would also push back on the idea that meeting our inflation objective requires a reaction from any particular set of prices, for example prices for AI-related technology goods," Schmid said. "Both narratives — that inflation is being driven by either supply shocks or by demand that is impervious to higher interest rates — have a common core," Schmid said. "Mainly, that inflation is somehow beyond the Fed's power to control. I don't believe this to be true. The Fed does have the tools to address inflation and has the responsibility to achieve price stability. As Chairman (Kevin) Warsh said, we have work to do." ... On Saturday, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins said she supported a steady pace of modest interest rate increases because that path of action better manages economic uncertainties. When it comes to moving monetary policy to a tighter footing, "a steady, gradual path seems appropriate to me at the moment. But I'm open-minded," Collins told reporters at a conference held by her bank on housing issues in Boston. "I do see the risks as two-sided on the real side of the economy," Collins said, with inflation high and gains broadening throughout the economy, while the job market was stable and could accelerate. items.title: Oil edges up as Hormuz tanker incidents highlight shipping risks
items.excerpt: Published Mon, Nov 16 2026 3:32 AM EST ... Oil prices inched back up on Monday, after fresh tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz underscored risks to Middle East supplies, although shipments through the strategic waterway have largely recovered to pre-war levels. Brent futures Add To Watchlist were up 5 cents, or 0.1%, to $95.89 a barrel by 0757 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist (WTI) crude gained 9 cents, or 0.1%, to $88.65. Both benchmarks had fallen in early Asian trade, with Brent down as much as 1%. Oil closed lower on Friday as the market weighed signs of lower geopolitical risk from the US-Israeli war against Iran, now in its ninth month. The benchmarks fell 16% and 13%, respectively, the prior week. Two oil tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz that led to explosions, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Monday, after six tankers caught fire in similar incidents on Sunday and Monday. Reuters could not independently verify the report. The recovery of export flows from OPEC+ remains fragile, with "regional supply highly vulnerable to renewed disruption", said BMI analysts in a client note. "As such, physical constraints on production and exports, alongside fluctuations in the geopolitical risk premium, will continue to dominate price action until a settlement is reached between Washington and Tehran." High shipping rates are also putting a floor on oil prices, said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade. Rates remain high because of the risks tankers face carrying crude through the Strait of Hormuz and because the number of ships tied up shuttling oil through the waterway for transfer to other vessels has reduced the available fleet. Limiting price gains, the world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. "For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness. That shift in narrative is clearly dampening the tone," said KCM Trade's Waterer. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand, the IEA said. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit.

items.title: ICYMI: Fed’s Jefferson says inflation is the key signal for rates, with PCE still at 3.6%
items.excerpt: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the path of inflation, rather than growth or jobs, will be the main guide for future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain well above the central bank’s 2% target. Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said further policy moves should be decided by carefully weighing trends in the data, the changing outlook and the balance of risks, ANI reported. He described inflation’s trajectory as the more important signal for setting the stance of policy. Figures cited in his speech showed headline personal consumption expenditures inflation at 3.6% in September, with core PCE, which strips out food and energy, at 3.1%. Jefferson said the October inflation data received so far point to price pressures staying well above target. He flagged energy as the main risk. Jefferson said he remains concerned that higher energy prices could lead to a broader and more persistent rise in inflation, noting that the effect is already visible in airfares and transport costs. Strong demand for new technologies is also lifting prices of some goods, including memory chips. By contrast, his assessment of the real economy was steady. Jefferson said labour market conditions have stabilised, with unemployment at 4.1% in October, a level he regards as consistent with maximum employment and expects to hold in the near term. The economy has gained momentum this year, he said, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4%, roughly in line with its potential. Jefferson said he voted with the majority to hold rates at the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting. Since then, he said, activity and the labour market have remained broadly solid, while inflation readings have continued to show persistent pressure.

items.excerpt: Financial markets had another volatile week as higher-than-expected U.S. inflation increased expectations of further interest rate hikes. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% in October, down from 0.6% in September but above forecasts of 0.3%. U.S. bond yields rose following the inflation data, strengthening the U.S. dollar and weakening gold prices. Several Federal Reserve officials said inflation remained too high and that further interest rate hikes were needed. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 0.50 percentage point rate hike could be appropriate. By Friday afternoon, markets were fully expecting a rate hike in December, with around a 10% chance of a larger 0.50 percentage point increase, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

items.title: U.S. attorney warns Sen. Elizabeth Warren against investigating Trump associates
items.excerpt: Nov. 16, 2026, 12:43 AM EST By Casey Wooten A Justice Department official on Sunday accused Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., of intending to target private individuals close to President Donald Trump with investigations. The allegation came in a letter similar to others sent to congressional Democrats. U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz sent a letter to Warren — who is likely the incoming chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee — calling on her to preserve documents related to investigations of Trump allies. Reitz noted that Warren appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates.” Reitz referenced a Nov. 11 letter in which Warren, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., asked Meredith O’Rourke, a National Park Foundation board member and top fundraiser for Trump, to retain documents related to funding for the White House ballroom and other projects. Reitz accused the three lawmakers of “demanding sweeping information about her and other private citizens and entities who associate with President Trump.” The letter to Warren signals an expansion of Reitz’s inquiry into congressional Democrats tasked with government oversight. When Democrats take control of Congress next year, Garcia is likely to take the gavel of the House Oversight Committee, while Blumenthal is expected to lead the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs’ Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. Last week, the White House issued a threat to congressional Democrats against probes into the administration. Since their midterm victories, Democrats have said Trump family businesses and immigration enforcement are some of their top targets for investigation. Reitz’s letter referenced an op-ed from Warren earlier this month in Time magazine, in which the senator wrote, “With astonishing brazenness, Trump has attempted to reengineer the federal government into a corruption machine designed to rake in profits for himself, his family, and his cronies.” Reitz also accused Warren of planning to target businesses that associate with Trump, referencing an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation” in which Warren said tech CEOs, Wall Street executives and giant corporations who have broken the law “better get ready for some investigations — serious ones.” “The context sends a strong smoke signal: you intend to target private individuals close to President Trump,” Reitz said. A spokesperson for Warren did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday night. Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has sent similar letters to Blumenthal and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., warning them against investigating Trump associates and calling on them to preserve documents. Reitz posted his letter to Warren on X, and Trump reposted it to Truth Social later Sunday.

items.title: 'Ebenezer,' 'Ramayana' Lead as 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Hits $100 Million
items.excerpt: Nov 16, 2026 12:22am PT # Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer,’ ‘Ramayana’ Dominate Global Box Office as ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Crosses $100 Million By Naman Ramachandran ... Johnny Depp’s return in Paramount’s “ Ebenezer” won the global box office this weekend, edging out Indian powerhouse “ Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” to claim the worldwide crown, while Toho’s “ Godzilla Minus Zero” crossed the $100 million milestone. Directed by Ti West, “Ebenezer” debuted at No. 1 globally with a worldwide weekend estimate of $42 million. The dark reimagining of Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” opened at the top of the North American chart with $19 million across 3,535 locations, while international audiences delivered a stronger $23 million debut across 63 markets. Audiences largely embraced Depp’s turn as Ebenezer Scrooge alongside an ensemble cast featuring Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Tramell Tillman and Ian McKellen. Exit polling yielded an “A-” CinemaScore, a 90% Verified Hot Popcornmeter rating on Rotten Tomatoes and 4.5 out of 5 stars on PostTrak (including 85% total positive and 66% definite recommend scores), with 51% of surveyed moviegoers citing Depp as their primary attendance driver. ... Hot on “Ebenezer’s” heels, Namit Malhotra’s “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” retained the No. 1 international crown and took second place globally, surging to a $147.5 million worldwide cumulative gross after just 11 days in release – already making it the seventh highest-grossing Indian film of all time. Fueled by stellar word-of-mouth and brisk midweek business, the Nitesh Tiwari-directed epic enjoyed a phenomenal second-weekend hold, dropping just 34% for a $38.1 million global frame, including $32.6 million from international markets. ... Meanwhile, Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” continued its box office rampage, taking fourth place worldwide with a $15.6 million frame and pushing its global cumulative total past the $100 million mark to $104.8 million.

items.title: What to Stream: 'GTA VI,' 'Always Lalisa,' 'The Altruists' and 'Steps' | The Independent
items.excerpt: The Associated Press Monday 16 November 2026 05:01 GMT The long-awaited arrival of “Grand Theft Auto VI” and a new documentary about K-pop star Lisa are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you. Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: a John Madden biopic starring Nicolas Cage, the final season of “Yellowjackets” and the animated movie “ Steps.” New movies to stream starting Nov. 16–22 — Nicolas Cage gained weight and wore prosthetics to play football coach-turned-broadcaster John Madden in a new film from David O. Russell, streaming on Prime Video on Wednesday. Kathryn Hahn plays his wife Virginia, while Christian Bale plays Al Davis in “Madden.” — The Anthony Bourdain biopic “Tony” will be available on HBO Max starting Friday. The film, from director and cowriter Matt Johnson, stars Dominic Sessa as the late celebrity chef. In his AP review, Mark Kennedy wrote that it “is a coming-of-age tale for a modern culinary giant. Set over just a summer, it’s also clearly an appetizer. And like all first courses, it leaves you with a nice first taste — but still hungry.” — “Steps” reimagines the Cinderella story from the point of view of the evil stepsisters. The animated musical, streaming on Netflix on Friday, features a starry voice cast including Ali Wong, as the misunderstood stepsister, and Amanda Seyfried as Cinderella, as well as Daniel Radcliffe, Bette Midler and Peter Dinklage. — Coming to Netflix on Wednesday is the difficult family drama “Gentle Monster,” in which Léa Seydoux grapples with the realization that her husband and father of her child engages with online child sexual abuse. — AP Film Writer Lindsey Bahr New music to stream starting Nov. 16–22 — K-pop superstar Lisa’s Sony Music Vision documentary “Always Lalisa” will become available to stream on Wednesday when it debuts on YouTube Premium. In the film, director Sue Kim follows Lisa, whose real name is Lalisa Manobal, through a pivotal year as she launches her first solo album, 2025’s “Alter Ego,” forms her own management company, plays Coachella, sings at the Oscars and makes her acting debut in “The White Lotus.” Grab some popcorn, read AP’s interview with Lisa about the project and hit play. — Darius Rucker has had a career like few others: First, as the lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist of rock band Hootie & the Blowfish, and then as a solo country music superstar. (His cover of “Wagon Wheel” should be considered canon.) On Monday, a new documentary detailing his life and career, “Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie,” will debut on Disney+ and Hulu. It’s a remarkable story — for both the diehard fan and the curious viewer. — R.E.M. fans, listen up. On Friday, the legendary alternative rock band will release a 25th anniversary edition of the 2001 album “Reveal,” complete with “The Black Session Revealed,” a collection of 17 previously unreleased tracks recorded for Radio France in Paris in May 2001. — AP Music Writer Maria Sherman New series to stream starting Nov. 16–22 — “The Altruists,” Netflix’s eight-episode limited series, traces the rise and fall of crypto exchange FTX through the turbulent romance between founder Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), who ran its sister trading firm, Alameda Research. Boyle told The Associated Press that he was drawn to the relationship itself. “I feel like everyone has been in that thing where they love someone and they can’t communicate. I wanted to tell that story.” The pair’s schemes left an $8 billion hole in customer funds. Bankman-Fried remains in federal prison after his 2023 conviction, while Ellison, who took a plea deal and testified against him, was released in January. The series premieres Thursday. — The fourth and final season of the survival drama “Yellowjackets” returns Friday, on Paramount+ as the soccer team’s rescue nears. The survivors race to bury their sins before help arrives. Readjusting to civilization after 19 months in the wilderness won’t be easy, as secrets loom and consequences for their actions remain. — “Melania, The Series,” a two-episode docuseries on Prime Video, picks up where Brett Ratner’s “Melania” documentary left off. The first episode, “Family & Trust,” covers her preparations to return to the White House, and the second, “Pride & Honor,” begins just after the 47th Presidential Inauguration. Melania Trump is an executive producer. It premieres Friday. — The third season of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” arrives on Disney+ and Hulu on Friday. The new episodes adapt “The Titan’s Curse,” the third book in Rick Riordan ’s series. Walker Scobell returns as Percy, who is shown holding up the sky in the first teaser. The season has eight episodes and is released weekly. — A new British spy thriller called “Secret Service” follows MI6 officer Kate Henderson as a covert investigation turns up evidence that a high-ranking U.K. politician may be a Russian asset. Gemma Arterton stars in the five-part series, adapted from Tom Bradby’s novel of the same name. It debuts Sunday on MGM+. ... New video games to ... 16-22 — You may have heard that “Grand Theft Auto VI” is almost here. So what’s it about? Well, this is the story of Jason and Lucia, two young lovers with nothing better to do other than stealing cars, robbing civilians and running from the cops. When a simple job goes haywire, they find themselves enmeshed in a conspiracy that stretches across Rockstar Games' flamboyant version of Florida. If you’ve played in the “GTA” sandbox before, you know to expect plenty of violence, raunch, reckless driving and other socially irresponsible shenanigans — though apparently you can play basketball, pool and minigolf if you need a break from all the mayhem. Put the pedal to the metal Thursday on PlayStation 5 or Xbox X/S.
